title: Excel for Mac alt shortcuts not working: KeyTips and Option fixes for accountants
metaTitle: Excel for Mac Alt Shortcuts Not Working: KeyTips Fixes
description: Alt shortcuts do nothing in Excel for Mac? Turn on KeyTips in version 16.89 or later, pick Option, and use the fallbacks for older builds.
targetKeyword: excel for mac alt shortcuts not working
intro: Alt shortcuts do not work in Excel for Mac by default. Microsoft says the Windows-style ribbon letters, called KeyTips, work in Excel for Mac version 16.89 or later, once you turn them on and choose Option. This guide is for accountants who need that fix today, plus the fallbacks for older builds and for commands that have no letter.
tldr: KeyTips are the Windows-style ribbon letters, and Excel for Mac has them only in version 16.89 or later.
KeyTips are off by default on Mac. Turn them on, then select Option (⌥) to match the Windows Alt key.
Check your version first with Excel > About Excel. If it is older, use Help > Check for Updates.
On older builds, turn on Keyboard navigation in System Settings > Keyboard, then press F6 to reach the ribbon.
Some commands have no letter, so keep the mouse for those. Test every change on a copy of the file.

blocks.text: Excel for Mac does not use the Alt key the way Windows does. Its ribbon letters, called KeyTips, are off by default. Microsoft says they work in Excel for Mac version 16.89 or later, and you can set them to respond to Option. On Windows you press Alt, then tap letters. On a Mac you press and release Option, then tap letters the same way. That one change breaks habits you built on Windows.
Check your Excel version before you change anything

Open Excel and choose Excel > About Excel. Read the version number in the window. If it is 16.89 or later, KeyTips should be available. If it is lower, choose Help > Check for Updates and restart Excel. Microsoft ties the feature to the Excel version, so this number decides which fix you need.

blocks.text: The table is a shortcut, not the final word. Microsoft's support page is the authority, and the copy we read carries no date. Excel Campus wrote in August 2024 that KeyTips were still in beta and needed the Beta Channel. Check whether your build has moved past that stage before you assume it works.
Turn on KeyTips and pick Option

items: Open Microsoft's support page on using the keyboard with the ribbon, and find the KeyTips setting for Excel for Mac.
Turn KeyTips on. Microsoft says they are off by default to prevent accidental activation.
Select the Option (⌥) key as the activation key, so it matches the PC Alt key.
Open a copy of any workbook, press and release Option, and look for letter badges over the ribbon.
Press the letters one after another, not at the same time, and watch the command run.

blocks.text: The exact settings location can move between builds. Follow Microsoft's current steps, not a screenshot from an old blog post. If no badges appear after the setting is on, go back to the version check. The most likely gap is the build number.
A worked example: sorting a client list with the keyboard

Say a client list sits in columns A to D, and you want it sorted by balance. Turn KeyTips on, then press and release Option. Badges appear over the tabs. Press the letter over the Data tab. Then press the letter over the Sort command. Excel opens the Sort dialog. Choose the balance column, pick the order, and confirm.
The mouse route is Data > Sort. The keyboard route only saves time once the letters feel automatic. Practice on the few commands you use most, and keep the mouse for the rest.

These figures describe spreadsheet risk in general. They do not measure Alt shortcuts. We found no study that counts hours lost to failed Alt shortcuts or to ribbon hunting. Treat any time estimate as your own measurement, and say so when you share it with a team.
When a command has no letter or a feature has limits

Some Excel commands have no underlined letter, so no KeyTip exists for them. Excel Campus reports this limit. Advanced features have their own limits too. Excel Campus says Power Query, Power Pivot and VBA user forms have limitations on Mac, so expect mouse steps there. Keep the keyboard for everything else.

Excel Campus also says Paste Values is missing from Mac keyboard customization. You cannot assign your own key to that command. Plan a mouse or menu route for it, and write that route into your month-end checklist.
Mistakes that keep Alt shortcuts broken

items: Pressing Option together with a letter. That types a symbol instead of opening the ribbon.
Updating Excel but leaving KeyTips off, since they are off by default.
Reading an older guide that says the feature does not exist on Mac, then giving up. The Bricks guide, dated February 2025, says that.
Testing a shortcut change in a live client file. Use a copy, every time.
Expecting Control+F2 to act like Alt. It moves focus to the menu bar, and Bricks calls that route a bit rigid.
Trusting a vendor's claim about price or subscription tiers without checking the vendor's own site.

blocks.title: Test on a copy first
blocks.text: Keyboard changes affect how Excel reads your key presses. Try each new sequence on a copy of the workbook before you use it on a file that a client or a reviewer will see.
Third-party add-ons and what your firm allows

Accelerator Keys is a separate app, not part of Excel. Its guide says that after you install it and grant accessibility permissions, pressing Option in Excel runs the Windows sequence. Its example is Alt+H+O+I becoming Option+H+O+I. The vendor says the app needs macOS Big Sur or later and offers a free 14-day trial with no credit card.

Before you install anything like this, check two things. First, your employer's rules on software you may run on a work Mac. Second, what the permission lets the app do. Accessibility access is a deep permission. Your IT team can tell you what your firm allows.
On a recent build, Microsoft's own KeyTips may already cover what you need. Try the built-in route first. Only test a vendor after the built-in route fails and your firm says yes.
What Lazur can and cannot do with this problem

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ (Option and Command) to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not press Alt, Option, or any letter for you. It does not click buttons or operate Excel. It is not an add-in for Excel and it does not sit inside the ribbon. It points and explains, and you press the keys.
One caveat matters here. Lazur's hold shortcut uses Option too. Test that the two do not clash in Excel with KeyTips on before you rely on either during a deadline.
Client files and what gets sent to AI

Follow your employer's rules on client data before you ask any tool about a live workbook. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm may still say no, and that answer wins.
What to do next

Check the version first. Then turn on KeyTips, select Option, and practice on the commands you use each week. Keep the mouse for anything without a letter. For more Excel help for accountants on Mac, see [Excel for accountants on Mac](/for/accountants/excel).

faq.question: Why do Alt shortcuts not work in Excel for Mac?
faq.answer: Excel for Mac hides its Windows-style ribbon letters, called KeyTips, until you turn them on. Microsoft says the feature is off by default and works in version 16.89 or later. Once it is on, select Option to match the Alt key. Check your version first, since older builds do not have KeyTips.

faq.question: Does Option plus a letter open the ribbon?
faq.answer: Only after KeyTips are on and Option is selected as the activation key. With KeyTips off, Option plus a letter types a special character. That is how the Mac handles Option, so it is not a broken keyboard.

faq.question: My version is 16.89 but the letters still do not show. What now?
faq.answer: Check the KeyTips setting again, then restart Excel. The sources used for this guide do not explain a case where the setting is on and the letters still stay hidden. Ask your IT team or Microsoft support, and test any fix in a copy of the file.

faq.question: Does Control+F2 replace Alt?
faq.answer: No. Control+F2 moves focus to the menu bar, which is a different route. The Bricks guide calls it a bit rigid. Use it for menu items you know by name, and use KeyTips for ribbon commands.

faq.question: Can Lazur press the Alt or Option keys for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not press keys, click buttons, or operate Excel. It answers questions out loud, points at things with a circle and a label, and guides you one click at a time while you do each step.

faq.question: Is a third-party tool a safer choice than the built-in KeyTips?
faq.answer: Not by default. Built-in KeyTips come from Microsoft and need no extra app. A third-party app runs separately and asks for accessibility permissions. Check your firm's rules first, and test on a copy.

costs.title: Minutes lost to mouse hunting
costs.text: No study we found measures time lost to Alt shortcuts that fail or to hunting through the ribbon. So the number is yours to estimate. Count how often a day you reach for the mouse to find a Data or Home command. The median pay for accountants and auditors was $40.23 an hour in May 2025, excluding self-employed workers, per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Multiply your minutes by that rate to see what the habit costs.

costs.title: Error risk when you retype or switch
costs.text: Spreadsheet errors come from many sources, and keyboard mistakes are one of them. A 2015 survey of 101 accountants, commissioned by a software vendor, found 9% spend more than 30% of their time checking spreadsheets for errors. Another 58% of respondents called error frequency very high or fairly high. Treat these as self-reported figures, not measured error rates.

costs.title: Errors in the files you audit
costs.text: Field audits from 1995 to 2007 found errors in 88% of 113 operational spreadsheets, as quoted by Keyhole Software. Those audits are old, and the figure reaches this page secondhand. It is still a good reason to test any new shortcut on a copy of the file first.

costs.title: Your own tool budget
costs.text: Third-party fixes cost money, and vendors change their prices. Accelerator Keys says its page offers a free 14-day trial with no credit card. Check the vendor's pricing page before you assume a cost. Check your firm's software rules too, before you install anything on a work Mac.

causes.title: Option types symbols on a Mac
causes.text: On a Mac, Option is the key for special characters. Hold it with a letter and macOS types a symbol, not a command. The Accelerator Keys guide describes the same pattern, where Option plus a letter types characters instead of running a ribbon command. So the keystroke looks right, but Excel never sees a command.

causes.title: KeyTips are off by default
causes.text: Microsoft turned KeyTips off on Mac to prevent accidental activation. Until you switch them on and pick Option, the letters never show. The shortcut then looks dead, even though the feature exists in your build. This default explains many cases of the problem.

causes.title: Older guides say the feature does not exist
causes.text: Some guides say the Windows ribbon letters simply do not exist on Mac. The Bricks guide, dated February 2025, says that. Microsoft's support page says KeyTips work from version 16.89 onward. The two sources conflict, so check your version before you believe either one.

causes.title: Keyboard navigation is off in System Settings
causes.text: Microsoft says older builds need Keyboard navigation turned on in System Settings > Keyboard before F6 can move focus to the ribbon. That setting is off until you turn it on. Without it, F6 gives you nothing useful, and the ribbon feels unreachable from the keyboard.

fixes.title: Update Excel and confirm version 16.89 or later
fixes.text: Open Excel and choose Excel > About Excel to read the version number. If it is below 16.89, choose Help > Check for Updates, then restart Excel. Microsoft says KeyTips work only in version 16.89 or later, so this step decides whether the rest of this guide applies to you.

fixes.title: Turn on KeyTips and select Option
fixes.text: Open Microsoft's keyboard guide for the ribbon and find the KeyTips setting. Turn it on, then select Option (⌥) as the activation key. Microsoft says KeyTips are off by default, so this step is needed even on a new build. Test it in a copy of a workbook before you rely on it.

fixes.title: Use Keyboard navigation and F6 on older builds
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard and turn on Keyboard navigation. Then press F6 in Excel, repeatedly, until focus lands on the ribbon. Microsoft describes this route for versions without KeyTips. It is slower than KeyTips, but it gets you to the ribbon without them.

fixes.title: Use Control+F2 for the menu bar
fixes.text: Press Control+F2 to move focus to Excel's menu bar, then move through the menus with the keyboard. The Bricks guide calls this route a bit rigid. Use it for menu items you know by name, and do not expect it to match the Windows Alt sequences.

fixes.title: Consider a third-party add-on only after checking policy
fixes.text: Accelerator Keys is a separate app. Its guide says that after you install it and grant accessibility permissions, pressing Option in Excel runs the Windows ribbon sequence. The vendor says it needs macOS Big Sur or later. Ask your IT team before you install anything that asks for accessibility access on a work machine.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Check your Excel version
plan.text: Open Excel > About Excel and read the version number. If it is 16.89 or later, continue. If it is lower, run Help > Check for Updates, then restart Excel and check again.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Turn on KeyTips and select Option
plan.text: Follow Microsoft's current steps for KeyTips. Select Option as the activation key. Test in a copy of a workbook, not a client file, and confirm the letters appear over the ribbon.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set up the fallback routes
plan.text: Turn on Keyboard navigation in System Settings > Keyboard and practice F6 for the ribbon. Try Control+F2 for the menu bar. Note which route feels faster for each task.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write your own cheat sheet
plan.text: List the five ribbon sequences you use most, using only commands and no client data. Keep the list on a sticky note or in a plain text file on your desk for the next few weeks.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Decide on add-ons
plan.text: Only if the built-in routes fail, check your firm's software rules. Ask IT before installing a third-party app that needs accessibility access, and test any tool on a copy first.
